title: Canon and Gigue in D major
hook: Eight bass notes, played twenty-eight times, with one of the best-known tunes in the world above them.

painting.title: The Concert
painting.pairingNote: A woman with a bowed bass instrument and another at the harpsichord, in a Dutch room of the 1670s; the same two instruments that play the canon’s endless bass.

facts: Johann Pachelbel (1653–1706) was one of the most admired organists of his day. Born in Nuremberg, he worked in Vienna, Eisenach, Erfurt, Stuttgart and Gotha before returning home in 1695 as organist of St Sebaldus Church. He was a close friend of the Bach family and taught Johann Christoph Bach, the eldest brother of Johann Sebastian.

The Canon and its Gigue are written for three violins and [[continuo|continuo]]. Nobody knows when or why. The only surviving source is a copy made around 1840, now in Berlin. One scholar has suggested it was written for Johann Christoph Bach’s wedding in October 1694, which Pachelbel probably attended, but that is a guess.

The canon is built on a [[ground-bass|ground bass]]: eight notes, two bars long, repeated twenty-eight times without change. Above it the three violins play a strict [[canon|canon]], each entering two bars after the one before with exactly the same music.

For more than two centuries the piece was forgotten. It was first printed in 1919. A slow, lush recording by Jean-François Paillard’s chamber orchestra in 1968 started its fame; by the late 1970s it was everywhere, from weddings to advertisements, and its chord pattern has been borrowed by many pop songs.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a calm round that grows richer at every turn of the bass (I), then a quick dance to end (II).

movements.heading: Canon
movements.title: Canon
movements.summary: The low strings and harpsichord start a slow eight-note bass line, and it never stops. The three violins come in one after another with the same melody, so the music is a round, like “Frère Jacques”. Every two bars the bass begins again; above it the violins move from long notes to running notes to rushing scales and back, a set of [[variation|variation]]s that grows out of the round.

mainIdeas.name: The bass
mainIdeas.description: eight slow notes, stepping down and leaping back up, played by the low strings and harpsichord from the first bar to the last.

mainIdeas.name: The canon tune
mainIdeas.description: a calm melody in the first violin, copied exactly by the second and then the third violin, two bars later each time.

stops.hear: Low strings and harpsichord alone: eight slow, even notes
stops.happening: The [[ground-bass|ground bass]], two bars long. It will be heard twenty-eight times

stops.hear: One violin enters with long, calm notes; a second violin starts the same melody, then a third
stops.happening: The three-part [[canon|canon]] sets off, each violin two bars behind the one before

stops.hear: The violins break into quicker, flowing notes
stops.happening: The melody speeds up while the bass keeps its pace

stops.hear: Fast scales tumble down and up, passed from violin to violin
stops.happening: The busiest writing so far, still following the canon

stops.hear: A skipping, dotted rhythm, long-short, long-short
stops.happening: A new pattern, copied from violin to violin

stops.hear: Notes land off the beat, as if the violins are hesitating
The violins jump up and down by wide leaps
stops.happening: The last new pattern before the end

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: The movement slows and settles on a long D major chord
stops.happening: The bass completes its last turn

notice: Listen only to the bass for a minute. It is the same eight notes every time; everything else changes around it.
Try to follow one violin’s melody and hear it echoed two bars later by the next.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The English Concert play period instruments, and Pinnock takes the canon at a flowing pace. Paillard’s 1968 version, the one that made the piece famous, is much slower and adds parts of its own. On the Spotify album the Canon and Gigue are tracks 1–2, followed by other Baroque favourites, among them Handel’s *Arrival of the Queen of Sheba*.

movements.heading: Gigue
movements.title: Gigue
movements.summary: A short, fast dance in a skipping rhythm, its beats divided into threes. There is no repeating bass here: the violins chase each other in imitation, like a lively [[fugue|fugue]] in miniature. It has two halves of ten bars, and each half is played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The gigue tune
mainIdeas.description: a quick, leaping phrase thrown from one violin to the next.

stops.hear: A quick, bouncing tune in one violin, taken up by the others in turn
A new phrase, again passed from voice to voice
The second half once more, to the final chord

notice: After the slow, patient canon, notice how quickly the gigue is over: about a minute and a half.

threads.title: Repetition
threads.body: Both movements depend on things coming back: the bass in the canon, the imitation and the repeats in the gigue. The pleasure is in hearing what changes when so much stays the same.

threads.title: A pair, not a single piece
threads.body: Pachelbel wrote the canon with a gigue to follow it. The gigue is usually left out today, but it was part of the plan: a slow piece, then a quick dance.

threads.title: A late fame
threads.body: A piece by a famous organist that nobody played for two hundred years became, through one recording in 1968, one of the most familiar pieces of classical music.
